name: San Juan River
reach: Sand Island to Clay Hills Crossing
agency: Bureau of Land Management, Monticello Field Office

camps.desc: Navajo Nation land: a Navajo permit is required to camp.

camps.name: 49.7 Mile

camps.desc: Navajo Nation land: a Navajo permit is required to camp.

camps.desc: Navajo Nation land: a Navajo permit is required to camp.

camps.desc: Navajo permit required.

camps.name: 61.5 Mile
camps.desc: Small. Several unremarkable small camps follow until Government Camp.

camps.name: 62 Mile
camps.desc: Small.

camps.name: Government
camps.desc: Navajo land, with no shade. The last camp before BLM reservations are required.

camps.name: Slickhorn A
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. Slickhorn is one of nine designated camps below Government Rapid.

camps.name: Slickhorn B
camps.desc: BLM reservation required.

camps.name: Slickhorn C
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. One of the larger, preferred sites, next to D.

camps.name: Slickhorn D
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. One of the larger, preferred sites, next to C.

camps.name: Slickhorn E
camps.desc: BLM reservation required.

camps.name: Grand Gulch
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. On a shelf just below Grand Gulch; at low water park at the downstream end. Good wash access.

camps.name: Trimble
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. Small.

camps.name: Oljeto Wash
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. Small, with big views. Not on Navajo land, but hiking up the canyon enters it and needs a permit. Flash-flood caution: a large drainage. False Oljeto, just upstream, is not the real one.

camps.name: Steer Gulch
camps.desc: BLM reservation required. The last camp before the take-out. Flash-flood caution.

rapids.name: Four Foot Rapid
rapids.desc: The first true riffle. Watch the rock on the left at low flow.

rapids.name: Eight Foot Rapid
rapids.desc: Boulder-strewn; scout from river left. Left-bank camping is closed here to protect bighorn sheep.

rapids.name: Ledge Rapid
rapids.desc: Named for a shelf on the left bank. Run right to avoid shallowing.

rapids.name: Gypsum Creek Rapid
rapids.desc: The steepest rapid on the trip. Take the left channel and work right, watching the left shore. Harder at low flow.

rapids.name: Twin Canyon Rapid
rapids.desc: Run left at all flows. Scout at low flows, when boulders block the right channel. American Whitewater rates it III-.

rapids.name: Ross Rapid
rapids.desc: Named for Kenny Ross, an early San Juan outfitter. Watch the rocks at the bottom.

rapids.name: Government Rapid
rapids.desc: The last rapid. A short boulder garden with a debris fan from the river-left canyon. Scout from river left.

hikes.name: Sand Island petroglyphs
hikes.desc: A petroglyph panel under a mile upriver of the launch, near the campground.

hikes.name: Moki Steps
hikes.desc: Ancient toe holds in the wall, visible from about 100 yards downstream. Look, but stay off them.

hikes.name: Butler Wash petroglyphs
hikes.desc: A petroglyph panel reached by walking upstream from the wash. Camping is closed here.

hikes.name: Lower Butler Wash petroglyphs
hikes.desc: More rock art, directly below the island.

hikes.name: River House ruin
hikes.desc: A 14-room 13th-century pueblo ruin about a quarter mile from the river. A must-stop. Do not climb on the walls.

hikes.name: Chinle Creek
hikes.desc: Hike up the wash from the camps on this bank. Navajo permit required.

hikes.name: Mendenhall's Cabin
hikes.desc: Trail starts on the far side of the saddle across the Mendenhall Loop. An easy hike with views.

hikes.name: Honaker Trail
hikes.desc: A clearly marked historic trail to the rim, about 1,200 ft of climb over roughly 2.5 miles. It starts at the lower end of Honaker camp.

hikes.name: Slickhorn Gulch
hikes.desc: The most-cited hike on the river: plunge pools and hanging gardens, with a swimming pool up the gulch. A longer hike reaches Trail Canyon, about 7 miles round trip.

hikes.name: Grand Gulch
hikes.desc: A "must-stop" side hike up a well-known canyon. Watch for flash floods.

history: Ross Rapid is named for Kenny Ross, an early outfitter on the San Juan.
Butler Wash is named for John Butler, a member of the 1879 San Juan expedition.
Below Mexican Hat the river doubles back on itself in tight, entrenched bends. Goosenecks State Park looks down on them from the rim.
When Lake Powell backs water up the canyon, the silt the river carries settles out and fills the channel, which is why the current dies below Government Rapid.

rules.d: A properly sized Type I, III or V life jacket for each person. Type II is legal in Utah but BLM strongly advises against it. One planning guide reports that everyone aged 13 or older must wear theirs at all times until below Slickrock Canyon, and children under 13 always.
A first-aid kit, a repair kit for every type of boat, and a boat pump for each type of boat.
One extra oar, paddle or motor for rafts, dories and canoes. One extra paddle per three kayaks, stand-up boards or inflatable kayaks.
An approved portable toilet system. Pack all waste out.
A fire pan is required even if you use a camp stove, except on one-day trips between April 1 and October 31.
Bring all your drinking water: about 1 gallon per person per day. The river carries about 25 million tons of sediment a year and clogs most filters. The only potable water is at Sand Island.
Below about mile 65 the current dies and the river braids across mud bars. Large rafts can hang up, especially from Slickhorn to Clay Hills.
Side canyons such as Grand Gulch, Slickhorn, Oljeto and Steer Gulch drain large areas. Camp above the high-water line and watch the sky.
Afternoon up-canyon winds are common in the lower section, and summer heat is severe. Plan to cover ground in the morning.
Wear a wetsuit and booties from spring through early summer.
Service is unreliable. A satellite phone or messenger is recommended. San Juan County Sheriff: 435-587-2237.
Do not touch petroglyphs, climb on ruin walls or stand on the Moki steps. Leave artifacts where they lie.

landmarks.name: Sand Island boat ramp
landmarks.desc: Put-in. A paved ramp with toilets and water. The only drinking water on the river. The campground can be booked on Recreation.gov.

landmarks.name: Highway 191 bridge
landmarks.desc: There is no other bridge until Mexican Hat.

landmarks.name: Tiger Wall
landmarks.desc: A striped sandstone cliff that forces a sharp right turn.

landmarks.name: Barton's Trading Post
landmarks.desc: Listed in river logs at this bend on river right.

landmarks.name: Chinle Creek confluence
landmarks.desc: The river splits just above the confluence and can look like a braided stream.

landmarks.name: Left-bank camping closure
landmarks.desc: Camping on river left is closed from here to mile 19.9 to protect bighorn sheep.

landmarks.name: Mexican Hat boat ramp
landmarks.desc: Upper take-out and lower put-in. A large gravel bar; no water and an outhouse. Park at the private lot uphill in town; cars have been broken into at the ramp.

landmarks.name: Mexican Hat bridge
landmarks.desc: Highway 163. Most of the town is visible just below.

landmarks.name: Mendenhall Loop
landmarks.desc: About 1.1 river miles around, but only about 450 feet across the saddle.

landmarks.name: Tabernacle
landmarks.desc: The peak marks the start of the Goosenecks, with the overlook of Goosenecks State Park above.

landmarks.name: Halfway Rock
landmarks.desc: A large rock seen from the Honaker Trail, close to halfway to Clay Hills.

landmarks.name: Start of reservations
landmarks.desc: From here downriver, BLM camp reservations are required for campsites on both banks.

landmarks.name: Flatwater and sandbars begin
landmarks.desc: Lake Powell sediment has filled the channel and the current ends. The river drops under about 1 ft per mile to the take-out. Large boats can hang up on mud bars.

landmarks.name: Whirlwind Draw
landmarks.desc: The last big draw before the take-out.

landmarks.name: Final straightaway
landmarks.desc: About 2.75 miles to the boat ramp. Shifting sandbars; sand waves can reach about 10 ft.

landmarks.name: Clay Hills boat ramp
landmarks.desc: Take-out. A toilet only, with no trash service or water. At low levels a trailer may not reach the water. Piute Farms waterfall lies downstream; do not continue past the ramp.

access.name: Bluff
access.note: Nearest town to Sand Island; permits and shuttle services

access.name: Sand Island
access.note: Put-in. Ramp, campground, toilets and water

access.name: Mexican Hat ramp

access.name: Clay Hills

permit.status: Required year-round · lottery April 15 to July 15

items.d: A permit is required year-round on the river between Montezuma Creek and Clay Hills, and you must hold it before arriving at the ramp. Permits are for private groups only; commercial and organized groups need a BLM Special Recreation Permit.

Apply on Recreation.gov from December 1 to January 31 (11:59 p.m. Mountain). Results come out February 14. Winners must accept and pay by March 15. Unclaimed dates and cancellations are released on March 16.

items.t: Before the lottery season: January 1 to April 14
items.d: Reservations open December 1 at 8 a.m. Mountain. Cancellations are released within 24 hours.

items.t: After the lottery season: July 16 to December 31
items.d: Reservations open March 16 at 8 a.m. Mountain.
An alternate permit holder can be added only on the lottery application or at purchase outside the lottery season. BLM will not add one by phone or email.
You can print it 14 days before launch. Gear is inspected at the put-in.
For launches five days away or less, and for Montezuma Creek to Sand Island, call the River Desk at 435-587-1544.

If you exit at Clay Hills you must reserve at least one campsite, and may reserve up to two nights, in the nine designated sites below Government Rapid (about mile 65). The first night must be at Slickhorn A through E; the second must be downstream of Slickhorn. Sites cannot be reused or shared without written BLM approval.
Submit camp preferences online when you book. They cannot be submitted by phone or email. If you give none, BLM assigns sites, usually within five days.
No camp reservations are needed on river right. A camp on river left is Navajo Nation land and needs a Navajo permit.

Camping on river left from Montezuma Creek to Trimble Camp, and any hiking or visiting of archaeological sites there, needs a Navajo permit. Call the Navajo Parks and Recreation office at 928-871-6647 well ahead; turnaround can be as short as 3 days. Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park: 435-727-5871.
Camping on river left is closed from about mile 18.1 to 19.9 to protect bighorn sheep.
$6, non-refundable, on every lottery application and reservation.
Sand Island to Mexican Hat $10. Mexican Hat to Clay Hills $20. Sand Island to Clay Hills $30. Montezuma Creek to Sand Island is free.
Per-person fees apply to launches March 1 to October 31. There are none for launches from November 1 to the end of February.
Reported at $10 to $15 per night on Recreation.gov. It is useful for the night before launch.
Up to 25 people, all ages counting toward the limit and the fees.
Pets are not allowed between Sand Island and Clay Hills. Service animals must be preauthorized by the Monticello River Office.
Cancelling or reducing the group 15 or more days before entry is refunded. There is no refund 14 days or less before entry, even for poor flows or weather.
Group size can change until 5 days before entry, before the permit is printed. A change of date or segment means cancelling and rebooking. Changes less than 5 days out must be made by phone.
One planning guide reports a limit of 75 people per day launching from Sand Island. Confirm with BLM.
